newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Futures seen playing up S.African shares next week.
newsitem.headline: Futures seen playing up S.African shares next week.

text.p: South African industrial shares are seen holding up well next week as futures players mount a bigger incursion into the unpredictable cash market.

Doubting the stock market's strength amid a drought of positive fundamentals, dealers and portfolio managers said futures-driven trade was the main reason for equities moving up. This trend would likely continue in the short-term.

"This firm trend will continue. The futures-driven trend will continue but other than that there is not much positive news. It remains a day-to-day market," said David Shapiro, a managing director of brokers Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.
The Johannesburg Stock Exchange's recent fickle relationship with Wall Street more or less removed that market temporarily as key determinant of South African shares' activity.
"Jo'burg's relationship to Wall Street is very confusing -- one day it tracks it and the next day it blatantly ignores it," said Greg Amoils, portfolio manager at Irish and Menell Rosenberg.

But commentators emphasised that the U.S. market would never fully lose its sway over South African shares and that U.S. economic indicators this past week still raised the spectre of another interest rate hike there which boded ill.

"We remain driven by Wall Street and there is still concern about Wall Street. Figures coming out from there still point to a possible interest rate hike. But as long as it holds, our market will be fine," Shapiro said.

The gap between local futures and their underlying stocks was widening and arbitrage trade could soon close this, taking share prices up with it, commentators said. They added that short-covering was also being seen.
"There is a lot of futures play. A lot of people seem to have been caught short and much of this strength is classic short-covering," Amoils said.

The only fundamental seen offering some support to shares was the current strength in the local bond market. The key R150 broke through the important psychological 15 percent barrier late Thursday and maintained a strong run on Friday morning.
But there was a lack of conviction among equity players as to whether this would hold.
"The strength in the bond market is confusing. I don't know whether it can hold its momentum and give equities enough of a kick," Shapiro said.

Gold shares were also holding up pretty well but dealers said their future would obviously remain as unpredictable as the bullion price which, although back above $340 an ounce, fell through that support earlier this week.

A dismal start to the first quarter gold results on Thursday cast a tiny shadow over the market, commentators said but emphasised that the worst had been expected for some time and much impact had already been discounted.
"Gold Fields was a disaster but the market reaction hasn't been too severe and this is quite positive for golds overall," Shapiro said.
An unpredictable market such as this left is vulnerable to jobbers which were snatching the opportunity to speculate and would continue active as long as it remained uncertain.
"It's a very choppy market and doesn't know what it wants to do. It's an unpredictable market, a proper professionals' market," Amoils said.
Economic indicators due next week are March consumer price inflation, money supply and private sector credit growth. But these were not expected to have much impact on the stock market.
Companies due to post results next week include Boland Bank on Wednesday and Adcock Ingram on Thursday.
